## Proof

Since $v$ is absolutely continuous on $[0,1]$ with $v(1)=0$, we have the integral representation

$$v(x) = v(1) + \int_1^x v'(t)\,dt = -\int_x^1 v'(t)\,dt.$$

Applying the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to this integral,

$$|v(x)| = \left|\int_x^1 v'(t)\,dt\right| \le \left(\int_x^1 |v'(t)|^2\,dt\right)^{1/2}\!\left(\int_x^1 1^2\,dt\right)^{1/2} = \left(\int_x^1 |v'(t)|^2\,dt\right)^{1/2}(1-x)^{1/2}.$$

Dividing both sides by $(1-x)^{1/2} > 0$ (for $x<1$),

$$\left|\frac{v(x)}{(1-x)^{1/2}}\right| \le \left(\int_x^1 |v'(t)|^2\,dt\right)^{1/2}.$$

Since $|v'|^2 \in L^1[0,1]$ (i.e. $\int_0^1 |v'(t)|^2\,dt < \infty$), the integral $\int_x^1 |v'(t)|^2\,dt$ is the tail of an $L^1$ function, and therefore

$$\lim_{x\to 1^-}\int_x^1 |v'(t)|^2\,dt = 0.$$

By the squeeze theorem,

$$\lim_{x\to 1^-}\left|\frac{v(x)}{(1-x)^{1/2}}\right| = 0,$$

hence

$$\lim_{x\to 1^-}\frac{v(x)}{(1-x)^{1/2}} = 0.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
